extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / English gentlemen and polite society (early 18th-century audience interested in manners, friendship, health, and conversation)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and prescriptive rules for behaviour in polite society: etiquette of a great man's levée, rules for friendship and love, regimen for health (temperance), and norms for civil conversation and argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of a Levée
rubrics_metrics.description: The Business of a Levée is to receive the Acknowledgments of a Multitude, that a Man is Wise, Bounteous, Valiant and Powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Levée is presented as a public spectacle in which the patron's virtues are signalled to many at once. The text describes the backstage orchestration (porters, valets, whispered cues) and implies that the practice often values outward show over substantive business; reforming this could incline the great to regard business rather than ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levée appearance and modes of opening
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several ways of making the first appearance: either half dressed and washing yourself (stately, peculiar to military men), or more reserved (civil officers buttoned up).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts military 'open-breasted' grace with the civil 'chastity of deportment,' noting the difference without prescribing a single correct mode—observing that different professions have conventional manners of appearance at courtly mornings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patron's conduct in a Levée (keep in generals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patron should often answer aloud in short, general phrases (e.g. 'It is well', 'I am of your opinion', 'You may be sure of my part in it') and 'keep in generals', leaving particulars unaddressed or hastened over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patron is typically placed centrally, keeps silence and order, gives brief answers suitable to many capacities, and avoids engaging in particulars—this allows him to appear informed and obliging to many petitioners in quick succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client behaviour and servility at Levée (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clients adopt servile airs—rising early, dressing to bow to a man in court-favour, seeking a small smile as proof of being engaged in his interests—often surrendering possession of their own minds in pursuit of outward show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay critiques such servility as a farce that imposes on both idol and idolater; it treats excessive outward show as a vice and implies that real happiness and purposeful use of time are preferable to slavish courtship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer business over ostentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The commerce between the mighty and their slaves (the Levée) might be so represented as to incline the Great to regard Business rather than Ostentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting the Levée realistically could encourage great men to focus on substantive affairs. The text urges that time be used for business and discourages vain applications and addresses that aim only at show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity and attentiveness in friendship and love
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglecting to visit an agreeable friend is punished by the transgression itself; in love, lack of reciprocal small kindnesses and attentiveness (being grave to mirth, inattentive to discourse, or interrupting) causes deep uneasiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The letter examples stress that small outward tokens of tenderness or attentiveness (avoiding secrecy, being frank about visits) are sufficient to reassure and prevent jealousy; carelessness that leaves a partner anxious is blamed even if not morally culpable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation and secrecy in intimate relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Women (or partners) who neglect to convince their husbands of innocence or love—who carry ordinary acts as if secret, or dally with a husband's anxiety—deserve misinterpretation and create unhappiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance is to avoid coquetries and affected indifference where small demonstrative behaviours would maintain mutual peace; transparency and little tenderness are advised as easy remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and reliability in friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid mercurial friendship—do not be capricious in appointments or behaviour; constancy across seasons and occasions is a mark of a proper friend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The almanack example (friend various by months, breaks appointments) shows how intermittent affections cause distress; the writer asks for assistance to reform such inconsistency into reliable companionship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance as a principal preservative of health
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance may in many cases produce the same effects as exercise and may, in some measure, supply its place where opportunities for exercise are wanting; it prevents superfluities and gives nature her full play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperance is recommended as practicable by all ranks, requiring no expense or time loss. It is presented as often superior to medicines, with historical examples (Socrates, Cornaro) cited to support its efficacy toward long life and resistance to disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diet rule: make a whole repast of one dish
rubrics_metrics.description: Make your whole Repast out of one Dish; if you indulge in a second, avoid drinking anything strong until you have finished your Meal; abstain from all Sauces, or at least such as are not the most plain and simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These practical rules aim to limit variety that solicits the palate and artificial provocatives that create false appetite. Following them reduces temptation to gluttony and the mixing of incompatible foods that disturb the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for drinking (Temple's quip)
rubrics_metrics.description: For drinking: 'The first Glass for myself, the second for my Friends, the third for good Humour, and the fourth for mine Enemies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted as a practical, memorable rule to avoid excess in wine. The counsel is to avoid all excess, particularly in common use of wine; the rule functions as an easy heuristic for temperate drinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Days of abstinence (fasting) as a restorative practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Man should have his Days of Abstinence... These are great reliefs to Nature, qualify her for struggling with Hunger and Thirst, often kill a Sickness in Embryo, and destroy the first Seeds of an Indisposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodic abstinence prepares the body for hardship, aids recovery, and can prevent incipient disease. It is recommended as a regular regimen suited to one's constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance and exercise reduce need for medicine and prolong life
rubrics_metrics.description: If men lived in an habitual course of Exercise and Temperance, there would be little occasion for medicines; many philosophers and Cornaro are cited as examples of longevity through temperate living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts luxurious modern meals with the simple diets of hunting peoples and philosophers, arguing that moderation and physical activity make medicines largely unnecessary and favor a long, comfortable life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for equanimity/tranquility rather than promised happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach people to be easy rather than to aim at absolute happiness: the lesson is Æquanimity, a Regularity of Spirit, a little above Cheerfulness and below Mirth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer advises practical, attainable calmness—cheerfulness maintained when out of pain and mirth accidental. Examples include modest pleasures (two old fellows smoking a pipe) that afford quiet contentment without philosophical affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote simplicity and domestic pleasures for the common man
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing domestic, plain life with its gratifications (simplicity, innocence, industry, temperance) will instruct those who need it most and render the fire-side of an honest artificer as entertaining as higher company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Spectator (writer) is urged to place such domestic relations 'in a handsome Light'—to make practical philosophy accessible to plain people and to show how ordinary virtues lead to tranquillity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disputes in conversation where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid Disputes as much as possible; it requires more Wit and more good Humour to improve than to contradict the Notions of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disputation for its own sake is presented as a conversational vice (common among lawyers). The guideline is to prefer improving or gently augmenting another's view to blunt contradiction that makes company unpleasant.

rubrics_metrics.name: When obliged to argue: use coolness and modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: If you must enter on an Argument, give your Reasons with the utmost Coolness and Modesty, two Things which scarce ever fail of making an Impression on the Hearers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cool, modest exposition makes one's case persuasive; examples show that calm reasoning and lack of dogmatism increase the audience's receptivity and esteem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dogmatism and excessive self-regard
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not be Dogmatical, nor show by actions or words that you are full of yourself; humility makes victory more acceptable and less envied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A non-dogmatic stance invites goodwill; acting as if one desires information rather than merely victory prevents alienating others and reduces envy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retreat gracefully and admit uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are pinched in your Argument, make your Retreat with a very good Grace: You were never positive, and are now glad to be better informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitting possible error or accepting new information preserves temper and reputation; the 'Socratic' approach (asking rather than asserting) helps avoid being caught in absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider opponents' biases; do not be angry at disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can be more unjust or ridiculous than to be angry with another because he is not of your Opinion; consider the Interests, Education, and Means by which Men attain their Knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask yourself what your opinion might have been with the biases of your adversary. Contention rooted in desire for victory or reputation is blameworthy; passion in argument obscures true reasons recollected later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek information, act as impartial moderator, and avoid pressing victory
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose to yourself the true End of Argument, which is Information; choose the part of moderator without engaging on either side; when you have gained a Victory, do not push it too far.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting as an impartial moderator garners esteem and reduces envy, gives chance to sift matters fairly, and allows one to show judgment. When victorious, restraint demonstrates generosity and prevents unnecessary humiliation of others.
